title: Chapter 5.  Polity & Governance — Article 371G & the Sixth Schedule

blocks.content: Mizoram's polity chapter is distinguished by Article 371G, one of the strongest special-protection constitutional provisions granted to any Indian state, directly negotiated as part of the 1986 Peace Accord — alongside Sixth Schedule autonomous councils covering its smaller tribal minorities.

Article 371G, inserted into the Constitution as part of the 1986 Peace Accord settlement (via the 53rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1986, the same Act that also provided for Mizoram's statehood), provides that no Act of Parliament shall apply to Mizoram in respect of: (a) religious or social practices of the Mizos, (b) Mizo customary law and procedure, (c) administration of civil and criminal justice involving decisions according to Mizo customary law, and (d) ownership and transfer of land — UNLESS the Mizoram Legislative Assembly, by a resolution, so decides.

This gives Mizoram one of the strongest state-specific constitutional protections of any Indian state — broadly comparable in spirit and legal structure to Nagaland's Article 371A (a similar provision negotiated as part of the earlier 1960s Naga settlement process, also protecting religious/social practices, customary law and land ownership) — and reflects the same core assurance (protection of land, customary practices, and social/legal autonomy) that has been the recurring central demand across nearly every North-Eastern insurgency-resolution negotiation covered across this book series.

★ EXAM POINT: Article 371G (Mizoram) and Article 371A (Nagaland) are structurally very similar 'sister' provisions — both protect land, religious/social practices and customary law from Parliamentary legislation without state Assembly consent, both negotiated as the culmination of a peace settlement — a frequently tested comparative-polity fact.

In addition to the state-wide Article 371G protections, Mizoram has three Sixth Schedule Autonomous District Councils specifically covering its smaller, ethnically distinct tribal minority communities in the state's border areas — a structural pattern of providing an ADDITIONAL layer of self-governance for minority tribal groups WITHIN an already tribal-majority state, worth noting as a further example of nested autonomy.

★ EXAM POINT: Mizoram's three Sixth Schedule ADCs (Chakma, Mara, Lai) protect SMALLER tribal minorities WITHIN the wider Mizo-majority state — a distinctive 'nested autonomy' structure, contrasted with Meghalaya's ADCs (companion volume), which cover the state's three MAJORITY community groupings instead.

cells: General (Dr.) Vijay Kumar Singh (Retd.), commonly referred to as V.K. Singh, former Chief of the Army Staff and Union Minister

Lalduhoma (Zoram People's Movement, ZPM), 6th Chief Minister of Mizoram, in office since 8 December 2023 — a former IPS officer, and notably the first Member of Parliament in India to be disqualified under the anti-defection law
ZPM won 27 of 40 seats, ending three decades (1989-2018 alternation, then Zoramthanga's MNF term) of alternating Congress-MNF dominance
Gauhati High Court has a permanent Bench at Aizawl (Mizoram does not have its own separate High Court)

items: Article 371G (inserted via the 53rd Amendment, 1986, alongside statehood): protects Mizo religious/social practices, customary law, and land ownership from Parliamentary legislation without Assembly consent — structurally similar to Nagaland's Article 371A.
3 Sixth Schedule ADCs for smaller minorities WITHIN Mizoram: Chakma ADC, Mara ADC, Lai ADC.
40-seat Assembly. Current CM: Lalduhoma (ZPM), since 8 Dec 2023 — first MP in India disqualified under the anti-defection law.
Gauhati High Court has a permanent Bench at Aizawl — Mizoram has no separate High Court of its own.
